extracted.intended_audience: Numberphile viewers, popular-math readers, and math communicators
extracted.subtask_description: A retrospective blog-series annotating Numberphile videos (here: the first year's playlist) with personal commentary, memories, links, and reflections on math communication. The post organizes videos in publication order and numbers annotations to make references easy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enjoyment / entertainment value
rubrics_metrics.description: "math doesn’t have to be useful to be fun."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value videos and content that make mathematics playful and enjoyable even when not directly useful; include fun artifacts, historical quirks, and surprising facts (example: video about 6174, YouTube '301 views' easter egg) to engage curiosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility / clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: "writing about math in a way where you don’t have to love math to understand it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for explanations and prose that non-experts can follow; use clear language, approachable examples, and writers/presenters (e.g., Alex Bellos, Simon Singh) who translate mathematics for a general audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal connection / anecdotal engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of personal memories, quotes, and emotional references (e.g., the author's memories of a friend, favorite quotes from presenters) to connect the reader to the material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate personal annotations, favorite quotes, and reminiscences to stimulate creativity and convey why the content matters to the author — this builds reader engagement and shows the human side of mathematical interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize content chronologically and referenceably
rubrics_metrics.description: "They are in order of publication date. The personal annotations are numbered by the video’s position in the playlist for easy reference."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present playlists or collections in clear order (chronological) and number annotations to make cross-reference and navigation straightforward; provide direct links to the playlist/video for reader convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide external resources and links
rubrics_metrics.description: The post links to the YouTube playlist, MathsJam site, Patreon, Ko-fi, and Paypal for further viewing/support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include links to original videos, supporting organizations, and ways to support creators so readers can explore primary sources and engage further; use links for context (e.g., event pages, related videos).

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight notable contributors and give credit
rubrics_metrics.description: Pointing out when specific contributors appear (e.g., "first video to feature Matt Parker", "first video with author Alex Bellos", "first video to feature Katie Steckles").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Call out guest presenters/authors and link to their work or profiles to acknowledge contributions and direct interested readers to further content by those creators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use notable quotes to emphasize importance or character
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotations are used to capture the tone or significance of content (e.g., James Grime: "You can tell this is an important theorem because it has a name. You can tell it is a very important theorem because it has a pompous name.").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select memorable or illustrative quotes from videos/presenters to encapsulate ideas or humor and to punctuate commentary; these help convey why particular segments stood out to the annotator.
